1:
Where the psalm comes from is settled two ways and left open by a third. Keil and Delitzsch dismiss the ascription in the old Greek as worthless and pronounce the psalm post-exilic, composed as mosaic-work out of earlier psalms and prophets and especially out of one prophet, so that it is entirely an expression of the religious consciousness which resulted from the Exile; twice over they say that we have here nothing but echoes of the older literature, and list the echoes verse by verse. Charles Ellicott reaches the same date from a single phrase, since the wide glance westward that takes in the isles and coasts of the great sea, and possibly more distant ones still, is characteristic of the literature of post-exile times. Adam Clarke leaves it open: there is no title in the Hebrew, fourteen manuscripts write the psalm as part of the one before it, and the versions differ among themselves in the titles they give it; who the author was is uncertain, though it is much in the spirit of David’s finest compositions, and many learned men suppose it written for the restoration from the captivity. Augustine of Hippo and John Calvin both refer the whole to Christ, Augustine taking the restored land for the resurrection of the flesh, after which all that the psalm sings was done, and Calvin arguing that the description does not apply to the kingdom under the Law and must predict the kingdom erected with the gospel.

What the clouds and darkness mean produces the sharpest exchange. John Calvin takes them plainly: a cloudy sky overawes us more than a clear one, and the psalmist uses the symbol to impress the world with the greater reverence of God. Others, he says, refine upon the words and make the clouds a check upon human rashness and presumption; this makes the words convey a very useful lesson, but he is against all refined renderings. Adam Clarke gives that refined reading in full: the subject cannot be comprehended because God is infinite, so there must be an impenetrable obscurity round about him. Charles Ellicott takes a third way, tracing the imagery to the appearance on the mountain and observing that the connection of the clouds with the foundation of the throne is peculiar to this poet and striking, since the immediate effect on the Hebrew mind of such a manifestation is not fear but a sublime sense of safety in the established right and truth of God. Matthew Henry keeps both together, granting that the dispensations are unaccountable and yet holding that a golden thread of justice runs through the whole web of the administration.

Adam Clarke builds the opening proposition on three divine names: the first signifies infinite and eternal being with unlimited power and, as Creator, universal government; the second marks the Director and Judge who shows men the difference between good and evil; the third the God who enters into a gracious covenant to enlighten our darkness and help our infirmity. C.H. Spurgeon and Matthew Henry both turn the multitude of isles homeward, Henry noting that his own country is a great isle with many belonging to it, and Spurgeon adding that upon actual islands some of the greatest victories of the faith have been won, instancing Polynesia and the kingdom of Madagascar, and remarking that many a land owes its peace to the sea, since if it had not been isolated it would have been desolated. John Wesley keeps the isles to the Gentile nations, and John Gill reports a Jewish reading that takes the melting hills for the kings of the wicked. Adam Clarke ends the passage by pointing out its figure, that the throne itself is animated and righteousness and judgment are made two intelligent beings who support it.
6:
The seventh verse produces the sharpest disagreement in the psalm, and it turns on who is summoned and who quotes the words. Adam Clarke answers both questions confidently: the one to be worshipped is Jesus, as the apostle says, and who will dare dispute his authority; and the gods are his angels, since so the old Greek renders it and so the apostle quotes it. Charles Ellicott denies both halves. The word is not to be rendered angels, as the old Greek has it, but is directly intended to include among superhuman beings the very agencies which the heathen nations worshipped as deities; and the quotation in the epistle, he adds, is made not from this verse at all but from the Greek of a passage in the law. Keil and Delitzsch agree on the second point and on the first, taking the clause of the superhuman powers deified by the heathen bowing down to him who alone is God in absolute personality, and likewise tracing the quotation in the epistle to the law rather than to this psalm.

Whether the verse commands or reports is a second question. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the verb is not an imperative at all, since as a command the clause would be abrupt and inconsequential, but the perfect of that which actually takes place. Charles Ellicott reaches nearly the same conclusion more cautiously: it is doubtful whether the verbs are to be taken as imperatives, though the old versions and our own do so, and probably a fact is stated. John Gill leaves the choice open between a prayer that the idolatrous nations might be enlightened and a prophecy that they shall be, since the words may be rendered that they are or shall be confounded. John Wesley keeps the wish, that they be ashamed of their folly, and C.H. Spurgeon the certainty, that they shall be so. Adam Clarke notices a play on the letters by which those who boast of idols are described as moving like madmen, which he refers to the violent gestures practised in idolatrous rites, and reads the word for idols as vanities or emptinesses, of men who make much ado about nothing. C.H. Spurgeon answers in his own coin, that a man who worships an image is but the image of a man and that one who boasts of an idol makes an idle boast, and then summons the heathen deities by name to lay down hammer and car at the foot of the cross.

What the heavens declare, and to whom, closes the entry. Adam Clarke makes them intelligent beings whose magnitude, number, revolutions, order, influence and harmony proclaim the skill and power of the Sovereign of the universe. John Gill offers three senses, the lightning and thunder as tokens of wrath, the inhabitants of heaven as the paraphrase and a Jewish commentator take it, and the ministers of the gospel whose work is to declare a justifying righteousness. Charles Ellicott corrects the number to all the peoples and draws the line back to his reading of the clouds, since at length the world at large is convinced by visible manifestations of what Israel had recognised through the veil of darkness and cloud. Matthew Henry makes the same double effect a figure: the kingdom is like the pillar of cloud and fire, with a dark side toward the one people and a bright side toward the other; and he observes that though the command was that the whole earth rejoice, it is only the sons of Zion and the daughters of Judah who do rejoice, for all should bid that kingdom welcome but few do. Adam Clarke takes the daughters of Judah for the villages of the land, with the city as their mother, and John Wesley for the people to whom the King came.
10:
The closing strophe forces a verdict on the whole psalm, and the two critics give opposite ones. Keil and Delitzsch, having called the earlier verses nothing but echoes, allow that this strophe is original, though they suspect it was perhaps not added till later; they read it as an encouraging admonition to fidelity in an age when a spirit of looking longingly toward heathenism was rife and steadfast adherence was threatened with loss of life, and note that those faithful in their confession bear here the name given them in a later persecution. Charles Ellicott answers the verdict directly: notwithstanding certain points of similarity between these verses and earlier psalms, the psalmist shows himself at the close more than a compiler, a true poet. He also prefers to point the opening words as a statement rather than a command, that they who love the Lord hate evil, in order to avoid an awkward transition in the clause following.

Whether the light is sown or risen divides them along the same line. Keil and Delitzsch say the beautiful figure has been misapprehended by the ancient versions, which read a rising where the text has a sowing; and the sowing, they add, is not a strewing into the earth but a strewing along the man’s way, so that the righteous advances step by step in the light, for which they cite a Greek verb used of the dawn and a line of a Latin poet on the first light of morning. John Gill reports the very reading they reject, that the old Greek and Latin and all the eastern versions and the paraphrase render that light is risen for the righteous; and he notes that light is frequently used by an old poet for joy and gladness. Adam Clarke keeps the sowing and makes it agricultural: the divine light in the soul is a seed which takes root and multiplies thirty and sixty and a hundred fold, as gladness is also a seed, so that we do not so much require more grace from God as the cultivation of what we have received, and God will not give more unless we improve what we have. John Wesley reduces the figure to a laying up in store, and C.H. Spurgeon expands it, since the night is almost over and the morning, advancing with rosy steps, is already sowing the earth with orient pearls.

On the command to hate evil the practical voices are agreed and one adds a witness from outside. C.H. Spurgeon holds that we cannot love God without hating what he hates, and that we are not only to avoid evil and refuse to countenance it but to be in arms against it. John Gill extends the hatred from sin to evil men, though to their actions and conversation and not to their persons. Adam Clarke grounds it in consistency, since evil is inconsistent both with God’s love to us and with ours to him. Charles Ellicott calls this a practical test of true religion which can never be obsolete, and quotes a dialogue in which Philosophy tells a satirist that love and hate are said to spring from the same source, and he replies that this should be best known to her, since his own business is to hate the bad and to love and commend the good, and that he sticks to it. Adam Clarke closes the psalm with two remarks: that all other joy is the mirth of fools, a luminous blaze for a moment that leaves nothing but smoke and ashes behind, and that the whole psalm has been taken by several of the ancient fathers of Christ and the last judgment, in which sense the reader may take it if he pleases.
